title: Design a Proximity Service (Yelp)
prompt:
Design the backend that lets a user open a map or type a query and see businesses near them: "coffee within 1 km", "open now, 4+ stars". Business owners can add and edit their listing, and people read details and reviews.

Assume about **200 million businesses** worldwide and **100 million daily users** who run roughly five searches each. Search results must come back in **under 100 ms**.
clarify: Is the search radius fixed or user-selectable (500 m to 20 km), and do we return exact nearest-K or any results inside the radius?
Are results ranked by distance only, or also by rating, popularity and filters such as category and open now?
How fresh must edits be: is a new business or changed opening hours visible in seconds or minutes?
Do businesses move? (Mostly no, which is what makes a static index possible.)
Is this one global deployment or per-region, and are reviews and photos in scope?

reference.requirements:
**Functional**
- `search(lat, lng, radius, category?, filters?)` returns ranked businesses
- CRUD on a business (owner), view a business with details and reviews

**Non-functional**
- Read-heavy (search : write well above 1000 : 1), p99 under 100 ms
- High availability; reads may be stale by minutes (eventual consistency is fine for edits)
- Dense cities and sparse countryside must both be fast
reference.estimation:
- Searches: 100M users × 5 / 86,400 s ≈ **5,800/s** average, ~**29K/s** at a 5× peak
- Business rows: 200M × ~1 KB ≈ **200 GB** (photos and reviews live elsewhere), so one machine could hold it, but not serve the QPS
- Geo index: 200M × (8 B geohash + 8 B id) ≈ **3.2 GB**, which fits in RAM on every search node
- Writes: even 1% of businesses edited a day is 2M/day ≈ **23/s**
- Insight: the index is tiny and almost static, so replicate it rather than partition it for capacity
reference.api:
```
GET  /v1/search?lat=&lng=&radius=1000&category=cafe&open_now=true&limit=20&cursor=
       → {results:[{id, name, distance_m, rating, ...}], next_cursor}
GET  /v1/businesses/{id}                  → full detail (cacheable)
POST /v1/businesses   PUT /v1/businesses/{id}   DELETE ...   (owner)
```
- Cursor pagination over a stable ranking; return distance computed server-side.
- Detail is a separate call so the search payload stays small.
reference.data:
- `businesses(id PK, name, lat, lng, geohash, category, hours, rating, ...)` in a sharded SQL or document store; the system of record.
- `geo_index(geohash_prefix, business_id)` for the search path, derived from the table above. A B-tree on `(geohash, category)` turns "same prefix" into a range scan.
- Reviews, photos and hours sit in their own services, keyed by `business_id`.
- Store several precisions (for example 4, 5, 6 characters) or derive them by truncating the prefix.
reference.design:
```
client ─▶ LB ─▶ search service ─▶ geo index (in-memory replicas)
                      │ └─▶ ranking / filters ─▶ business cache ─▶ business DB
owner ─▶ business service ─▶ business DB ─CDC─▶ index builder ─▶ geo index
```
- **Read:** compute the user's geohash at a precision whose cell is at least the radius, fetch that cell **and its 8 neighbours**, drop anything beyond the radius using real (haversine) distance, rank, and hydrate details from cache.
- **Write:** owner edits go to the DB; a change feed updates the index within minutes and evicts the cache entry.
- Index choices: **geohash** is a string prefix, so it works in any SQL or KV store; a **quadtree** splits cells until each holds at most N points, so dense areas get finer cells.
reference.deepdives:
- **Geo index and the boundary problem.** A geo cell groups nearby points, but two close points can sit in adjacent cells with different prefixes, so always query the 9-cell neighbourhood. Choose precision by radius: level 5 is ~4.9 km square, level 6 ~1.2 × 0.6 km. Geohash is simple but uniform: Manhattan puts thousands of businesses in one cell. Fix with a variable-depth prefix (re-query at one more character when a cell is too full) or a quadtree with a capacity per leaf. Also mention poles and the antimeridian.
- **Scaling and sharding.** Because the index is ~3 GB, replicate all of it on every search node and spread load by query. If it ever outgrows memory, shard by geohash prefix; a plain prefix leaves dense cities hot, so split hot prefixes further or use virtual nodes.
- **Freshness and caching.** Cache results per (cell, category, filters) with a short TTL, and the business detail by id. Edits are rare, so a few minutes of staleness is acceptable; bulk edits from a chain with 500 stores go through a batch job.
- **Beyond the radius.** Text queries go to a search engine (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) with a geo-distance filter; keep the geo index for the pure-map path.
reference.wrapup:
- Biggest decision: a precomputed cell index, read-replicated, instead of scanning or computing distance for every business.
- Trade-offs: geohash (simple, uniform, boundary handling) vs quadtree (adaptive, harder to update); replicate vs shard the index.
- Next: personalised ranking, multi-region replicas, moving entities (see nearby friends), map tiles served from a CDN.

rubric.text: States the workload is read-heavy and separates the search path from the rare owner-write path
Estimates search QPS and notes the geo index is small enough to hold in memory
Uses a geo index (geohash, quadtree, S2/H3) instead of scanning all businesses or computing distance for each
Explains geohash precision, prefix match and how precision is chosen from the search radius
Handles the boundary problem by querying the neighbouring cells and filtering with exact distance
Addresses uneven density (dense city vs rural): adaptive quadtree or variable-depth prefix
Scaling plan for the index: replicate it, or shard by prefix with hot-cell mitigation
Caches search results and business details and says how they are invalidated
Keeps the business table as the source of truth and updates the index asynchronously (eventual consistency accepted)
Covers ranking and filters (category, open now, rating) and cursor pagination
Edge cases: poles/antimeridian, bulk updates, fault tolerance (replica failover, multi-region)
